slides.title: Compute, memory and bandwidth
slides.text: Session 1 Compute, memory and bandwidth Estimate the FLOPs and bytes moved of a layer Place a layer on a roofline from its arithmetic intensity Name the binding limit of a described workload 01

slides.title: Every step is limited by compute, memory capacity or memory bandwidth
slides.text: What can make a step slow Every step is limited by compute, memory capacity or memory bandwidth Compute Floating-point operations per second the processor can do. A large matrix product runs into this roof. Capacity Bytes that fit at all. Too many and the run fails, or spills to slower memory. Day 2 is about this one. Bandwidth Bytes per second between memory and the cores. Elementwise layers and decoding one token at a time run into this roof. What goes wrong. Optimising the limit that does not bind. Fewer FLOPs do not help a step that waits for memory.

slides.title: Count FLOPs and bytes by hand: it takes two lines
slides.text: Before any timer Count FLOPs and bytes by hand: it takes two lines Layer FLOPs Bytes moved (float32) Intensity A · fully connected, batch 512, 1,024 to 1,024 2 x 512 x 1,024 x 1,024 = 1.07 G 4 x (input + weight + output) = 8.4 MB 128 FLOP/byte B · add a bias, then ReLU, on 4,096 x 4,096 2 per element = 0.034 G read and write each element = 134 MB 0.25 FLOP/byte Arithmetic intensity = FLOPs divided by bytes moved. It is a property of the layer, not of the machine.

slides.title: Attainable speed is the lower of two roofs
slides.text: The roofline idea Attainable speed is the lower of two roofs attainable = min(peak, intensity x bandwidth) Below the ridge point a layer waits for memory; above it, for arithmetic. Ridge point = peak / bandwidth The intensity at which the two roofs meet. A floor on time, never a promise: real layers sit under their roof. It tells you which roof to push: fewer bytes or fewer FLOPs. Batching raises intensity: the weights are read once for more rows.

slides.title: A thin laptop: 138 GFLOP/s, 33.7 GB/s, a ridge at 4.1 FLOP per byte
slides.text: Measured in Lab 1.1 on the course's laptop A thin laptop: 138 GFLOP/s, 33.7 GB/s, a ridge at 4.1 FLOP per byte 138 GFLOP/s, a 2,048-square matrix product, 4 threads 33.7 GB/s, a 256 MB copy 4.1 FLOP per byte at the ridge Layer A (128 FLOP/byte) is far above the ridge: compute-bound. Layer B (0.25) is far below: memory-bound. Measured: A 6.7 ms against a predicted 7.8 ms; B 6.9 ms against 4.0 ms.

slides.title: Data reused close to the cores is cheap; data fetched from main memory is not
slides.text: Caches and data movement Data reused close to the cores is cheap; data fetched from main memory is not Registers a few hundred bytes per core → L1 and L2 caches tens of kilobytes to a few megabytes → Last-level cache megabytes, shared → Main memory gigabytes, the bandwidth you measured Why the matrix product is fast. It works on tiles that stay in cache and reuses each number many times. The 256 MB copy cannot: it reads everything once.

slides.title: Each processor trades generality for throughput on dense arithmetic
slides.text: CPUs, GPUs and neural accelerators Each processor trades generality for throughput on dense arithmetic CPU Few strong cores with wide vector units. Good at branches, small batches and everything around the model. GPU Thousands of simple lanes and very high memory bandwidth. Needs large, regular work to stay busy. Neural accelerator Fixed-function units for matrix products in low precision, on many new laptops and phones. Needs a runtime that supports it. Same roofline, different numbers. Each has its own peak and bandwidth, so the same layer can bind differently on each.

slides.title: Time with a monotonic clock, around the call, many times
slides.text: Timers Time with a monotonic clock, around the call, many times ms = [] for _ in range(100): t0 = time.perf_counter() with torch.no_grad(): model(leaf) ms.append((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000) perf_counter never jumps; time.time follows the wall clock, which can be adjusted. On a GPU, call torch.cuda.synchronize() before reading the clock: the work is asynchronous. One timing is an anecdote. A hundred are a distribution.

slides.title: Latency has a floor and a long right tail
slides.text: Measured in Lab 1.2: one Waraqa inference, batch 1, 100 calls Latency has a floor and a long right tail 5.7 ms median 7.4 ms 95th percentile 8.4 ms 99th percentile Report the median and the 95th percentile. The mean is pulled up by the tail; a standard deviation assumes a bell curve that latency never has.

slides.title: The first call is a different event: report it, do not average it
slides.text: The first calls The first call is a different event: report it, do not average it 1.3 x the warm median, for the first call of a freshly loaded model (Lab 1.2) The first call allocates memory, picks kernels and fills caches. A user who opens the app pays it once; a benchmark that includes it in 100 calls hides both numbers. So: warm up, then time; and time the cold start on its own.

Write what else was running next to every number.

slides.title: Warm up, repeat, report percentiles and the conditions
slides.text: The rule for the week Warm up, repeat, report percentiles and the conditions 1 · Warm up untimed calls first; the cold start reported apart → 2 · Repeat at least 100 calls on fixed inputs → 3 · Summarise median and 95th percentile, later with intervals → 4 · Record processor, threads, power mode, what else ran

slides.title: A timer says how long; a profiler says what ran
slides.text: Timers and profilers A timer says how long; a profiler says what ran Timers Cheap, honest about wall time, blind to what happened inside. Put them around phases you name. Profilers Record every operator or sample every call stack. Show where time goes inside a phase, with some overhead of their own. Use both. Timers to find the slow phase, a profiler to find why it is slow, timers again to prove the fix.

slides.title: A training step has four phases, and any of them can be the slow one
slides.text: A training step A training step has four phases, and any of them can be the slow one 1 · Load read, decode, augment, batch → 2 · Forward compute the loss → 3 · Backward compute the gradients → 4 · Optimiser update the weights What goes wrong. Buying a faster processor for a step that waits for its data.

slides.title: Lina's step is input-bound: loading is the largest phase
slides.text: Measured in Lab 1.3: median of the timed steps, batch 64 Lina's step is input-bound: loading is the largest phase Loading 1,420 ms, 66% Backward 385 ms, 18% Forward 342 ms, 16% Optimiser 5 ms, 0.2% One step: 2,142 ms. One epoch of 16,000 leaves at this rate: about 9 minutes.

slides.title: Removing one phase can never beat the sum of the others
slides.text: The ceiling of a fix Removing one phase can never beat the sum of the others 2.9 x the most Lina's step can gain if loading cost nothing (Lab 1.3) Speed-up limit = 1 / (1 - share of the phase you fix). Compute this before you start: it says whether the fix is worth a day. After the fix, the next phase is the bottleneck: measure again.

slides.title: Fixing an input-bound pipeline
slides.text: Session 4 Fixing an input-bound pipeline Tell an input-bound step from a compute-bound one Add parallel loading and a cache of preprocessed data Measure the speed-up and say which change bought it 04

slides.title: A step is input-bound when the model waits for its next batch
slides.text: Input-bound against compute-bound A step is input-bound when the model waits for its next batch Input-bound Loading is the largest phase. A faster model changes nothing. Fix the pipeline. Compute-bound Forward and backward dominate. The pipeline is good enough. Days 2 and 3 work here. Signs. A GPU at low utilisation; one core at 100% while others idle; step time that does not change with model size.

slides.title: Decoding is compute too, and the file format sets its price
slides.text: Measured in Lab 1.4: one leaf, 50 decodes Decoding is compute too, and the file format sets its price Format of one leaf Decode ms Size kB PNG, 224 pixels (the field app's export) 1.85 119 JPEG quality 90, 64 pixels 0.17 1.4 JPEG is lossy: the two decoded leaves differ by 2.5 of 255 per pixel on average. Whether that matters is a quality question, measured, not seen.

slides.title: Workers prepare the next batches while the model trains on this one
slides.text: Parallel loading and prefetching Workers prepare the next batches while the model trains on this one DataLoader(ds, batch_size=64, shuffle=True, num_workers=4, persistent_workers=True, prefetch_factor=2) Workers hide loading behind compute; they do not make it cheaper. They take cores the training step also wants. On Windows and macOS each worker is a fresh Python process: the first batch is slow.

slides.title: Decode once, store the 64-pixel bytes, read bytes every epoch
slides.text: Caching preprocessed data Decode once, store the 64-pixel bytes, read bytes every epoch 50 MB for 4,096 leaves as one uint8 array, built once in 88 s (Lab 1.4) The cache is right when preprocessing is the same every epoch. It is wrong when augmentation must differ each epoch at full size, or when the data changes faster than the cache. What it changed besides speed. Lina rotated by any angle; the cache rotates by multiples of 90 degrees. A speed-up that changes what the model learns is checked for quality.

slides.title: The before-and-after table is the evidence, not the code change
slides.text: Measured in Lab 1.4, full mode The before-and-after table is the evidence, not the code change Pipeline Step ms Loading ms Speed-up Baseline (Lina) 1,059 343 1.0x 4 workers 1,001 1 1.1x Cache, main process 725 11 1.5x Cache, 4 workers 693 0 1.5x When loading is near zero the step is compute-bound: what is left is forward, backward and the optimiser.

slides.title: Loading vanished. Why is the step only a little faster?
slides.text: Checkpoint Loading vanished. Why is the step only a little faster? With four workers, the loading phase drops from 800 ms to almost zero, but the step goes from 2,900 ms to 2,200 ms. What explains it? The workers are not running It is timer noise; the real speed-up is larger Decoding became cheaper, but not by enough The rest of the step was always about 2,100 ms, and the workers take cores from it

slides.title: Where memory goes
slides.text: Session 1 Where memory goes Compute the bytes of weights, gradients and optimiser state Estimate activation memory from layer shapes and batch size Explain the gap between an estimate and a measured peak 01

slides.title: Training memory has four parts, and only one grows with the batch
slides.text: What a training step holds Training memory has four parts, and only one grows with the batch Weights 4 bytes per parameter in float32. Gradients One per weight: another 4 bytes. Optimiser state AdamW keeps two numbers per weight: 8 bytes. Activations What the forward pass keeps for the backward pass: grows with batch and image size. Rule of thumb. 16 bytes per parameter before any activation, for float32 and AdamW.

slides.title: Each convolution block keeps about two tensors the size of its output
slides.text: Estimate by hand Each convolution block keeps about two tensors the size of its output Block output (per leaf) Numbers 32 x 64 x 64, twice 2 x 131,072 64 x 32 x 32, twice 2 x 65,536 128 x 16 x 16 32,768 128 x 8 x 8 8,192 Sum, x 2 tensors x 4 bytes about 3.5 MB per leaf

slides.title: Activations dominate, and grow in proportion to the batch
slides.text: Measured in Lab 2.1: one AdamW step of Waraqa Activations dominate, and grow in proportion to the batch Batch Estimate MB Saved activations MB Measured peak MB 16 60 67 94 64 227 270 325 256 894 1,078 1,165 Saved activations are counted exactly by autograd hooks; the peak is the process's resident memory, sampled during the step.

slides.title: Each gap between estimate and measurement has a name
slides.text: Explain every difference Each gap between estimate and measurement has a name Estimate < saved Pooling indices (8-byte integers) and the input batch were not counted. Saved < peak Gradients of activations and convolution work buffers are alive during the backward pass. Small batches Fixed costs dominate: weights, optimiser state, the allocator's own reserve. LO3 evidence. The estimate table next to the measured peaks, with each difference explained in a line.

slides.title: Sixteen bits buy half the bytes and give up range or precision
slides.text: Number formats (recap of AE-202) Sixteen bits buy half the bytes and give up range or precision Format Bits Exponent / fraction Gives up float32 32 8 / 23 nothing: the reference float16 16 5 / 10 range: small gradients underflow to zero bfloat16 16 8 / 7 precision: the range of float32, fewer digits int8 8 integer with a scale both, recovered by calibration (Day 3)

slides.title: Autocast runs the heavy operations in 16 bits and keeps the rest in 32
slides.text: Mixed precision Autocast runs the heavy operations in 16 bits and keeps the rest in 32 with torch.autocast("cpu", dtype=torch.bfloat16): out = model(x) # convolutions in bfloat16 loss = F.cross_entropy(out.float(), y) loss.backward() # gradients flow back opt.step() # float32 master weights Mixed : weights and optimiser stay in float32; small updates would vanish in 16 bits. On a CPU, autocast defaults to bfloat16; on a GPU to float16. float16 needs a gradient scaler to keep small gradients from underflowing.

slides.title: float16 lost 2.9% of Hasad's gradients without a single error
slides.text: Measured: Hasad, one backward pass on 32 questions it already answers well float16 lost 2.9% of Hasad's gradients without a single error Layer group Entries Zero in float16 only Embeddings 26,496 10.67% Feed-forward 790,272 3.20% Attention 396,288 1.81% Norms 3,328 0.09% All 1,216,384 2.90% Loss 0.000415 in both runs, no infinity or NaN: not overflow. The same batch in float32 gives every one of these entries a nonzero gradient: not the learning rate. Gradients that are zero only in float16 fell below its smallest number, about 6e-8: underflow.

slides.title: A scale of 65,536 brings the lost gradients back; too large a scale overflows
slides.text: The fix: scale the loss, unscale the gradients A scale of 65,536 brings the lost gradients back; too large a scale overflows Loss scale Lost Inf or NaN Error vs float32 1 2.90% 0 12.23% 256 0.01% 0 0.34% 65,536 0.00% 0 0.30% 16.8 million 0.00% 0 0.31% 4.3 billion 0.00% 1.2 million unusable scaler = torch.amp.GradScaler("cuda") with torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.float16): loss = loss_fn(model(x), y) scaler.scale(loss).backward() # loss x scale scaler.unscale_(opt) # before clipping clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0) scaler.step(opt) # skipped on inf or NaN scaler.update() # adjust the scale PyTorch's scaler starts at 65,536, halves the scale and skips the step when it finds inf or NaN, and doubles it after 2,000 clean steps.

slides.title: Reduced precision is faster only where the hardware computes in it

slides.title: Four micro-batches of 64, one optimiser step
slides.text: Gradient accumulation Four micro-batches of 64, one optimiser step for xm, ym in zip(x.chunk(4), y.chunk(4)): loss = F.cross_entropy(model(xm), ym) / 4 loss.backward() # gradients add up in .grad opt.step() opt.zero_grad() Divide each loss by the number of micro-batches: the sum is the mean over 256. Activations of one micro-batch at a time: about a quarter of the memory. Costs time: four smaller calls do less work in parallel.

slides.title: Accumulation equals a large batch only for layers that treat each example alone
slides.text: Checked in Lab 2.3 Accumulation equals a large batch only for layers that treat each example alone Batch norm mode Largest relative gradient difference Evaluation (stored statistics) 3.8e-05 Training (statistics per batch) 1.2 With batch norm, each micro-batch is normalised by its own statistics. It usually trains fine; it is not the same computation.

slides.title: Keep a few activations, recompute the rest during the backward pass
slides.text: Activation checkpointing Keep a few activations, recompute the rest during the backward pass from torch.utils.checkpoint import checkpoint_sequential feats = checkpoint_sequential(model.features, 4, x, use_reentrant=False) logits = model.head(feats.mean(dim=(2, 3))) Only the boundaries of 4 segments are kept; each segment's inside is recomputed when its gradient is needed. Trades about one extra forward pass for memory. The idea is from Chen et al., 2016: memory that grows more slowly than depth.

slides.title: Separate operations read and write the whole activation each time
slides.text: Operator fusion Separate operations read and write the whole activation each time Convolution writes z → Batch norm reads z, writes y → ReLU reads y, writes y Fused. One kernel computes the convolution, the affine map and the ReLU while the data is still in cache: one write instead of three.

slides.title: At inference, batch norm folds into the convolution's weights
slides.text: One fusion by hand At inference, batch norm folds into the convolution's weights s = bn.weight / torch.sqrt(bn.running_var + bn.eps) W_new = conv.weight * s.reshape(-1, 1, 1, 1) b_new = bn.bias - bn.running_mean * s At inference batch norm is a fixed affine map per channel; a convolution is linear: the two combine. Not during training: the statistics change every batch. Outputs agree to rounding: largest logit difference 5.7e-06 in Lab 2.4.

slides.title: A compiler captures the graph, fuses operations and generates code once
slides.text: Compilation A compiler captures the graph, fuses operations and generates code once torch.compile(model): capture on the first call, then reuse the generated code. Its default backend generates C++ for processors: it needs a C++ compiler. Colab, Linux and macOS usually have one; the course's Windows laptop did not. Two numbers, always The first-call cost (capture and code generation) and the steady-state speed per call.

slides.title: A batch does not exist until its requests arrive
slides.text: The hidden cost A batch does not exist until its requests arrive average wait = (b - 1) / (2 x rate) plus the batch's own time. At 2 leaves per second a batch of 8 makes the average leaf wait about 1.75 s before computing starts. Office, 2 leaves per second: batch 1 is the only batch that meets the budget. slides.title: Store numbers as small integers with a scale, and map them back when needed
slides.text: Quantisation Store numbers as small integers with a scale, and map them back when needed real value = scale x (integer - zero point) 8 bits give 256 levels; 4 bits give 16. The scale is chosen per tensor, per channel or per block of weights. Smaller files : a quarter (8-bit) or an eighth (4-bit) of float32. Faster only where kernels compute on integers or blocks. Lossy : quality is measured again, by group.

slides.title: Static quantisation calibrates activation ranges on real data; dynamic computes them on the fly
slides.text: For a classifier Static quantisation calibrates activation ranges on real data; dynamic computes them on the fly Weights Activations Needs Static 8-bit, ahead of time 8-bit, ranges from calibration a few hundred representative inputs Dynamic 8-bit, ahead of time ranges computed at run time nothing; less speed on convolutions Quantisation-aware training training sees the rounding and adapts to it a training run

slides.title: Zeroing weights saves nothing on dense kernels; removing channels does
slides.text: Pruning Zeroing weights saves nothing on dense kernels; removing channels does Unstructured Set the smallest weights to zero anywhere. The matrices keep their shape: a dense kernel multiplies zeros as fast as other numbers. Structured Remove whole filters (channels). Every matrix gets smaller, so every layer does less work.

slides.title: Distillation trains the small model to imitate the large one's probabilities
slides.text: A third route, as a concept Distillation trains the small model to imitate the large one's probabilities The teacher's output says not only "rust" but "rust, a little like leaf spot". The student learns from those soft targets as well as the labels. Often beats the same small model trained on labels alone. When to choose which Prune when you own a trained large model and want a cheap result; shrink or distil when you train anyway and want the simplest artefact.

slides.text: Percentiles with intervals A bootstrap interval says how far the median could move on a re-run rng = np.random.default_rng(206) boots = np.percentile( ms[rng.integers(0, n, (2000, n))], q, axis=1) low, high = np.percentile(boots, [2.5, 97.5]) Resample the timings with replacement, recompute the percentile, 2,000 times. The middle 95% of those values is the interval. The 95th percentile's interval is wider: it rests on fewer calls.
